Good morning! I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a quick, 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. There are no right or wrong answers; we simply want to understand your emotional well-being so we can offer the best support. Everything you share stays confidential between you and our team. We’ll go at your pace, and if any question feels difficult, we can pause.

Let’s begin gently: Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has even pleasant moments felt flat or absent?

Good morning, Dr. Martinez. I guess… some things still feel nice—like when my little guy gives me that gummy smile or when I get ten quiet minutes with my coffee—but the spark isn’t quite the same. It’s kind of muted, like I’m going through the motions more than really feeling it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… most of the time I can still laugh. Like, my partner will make a dumb joke or the baby will make a silly face and I’ll chuckle. It’s not as hearty as before, but it does happen—maybe every couple of days.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still mark little things on the calendar—coffee with my neighbor, a walk to the park—but the excited feeling is kind of watered-down. I go more because I “should” enjoy them than because I truly can’t wait. When the moment arrives it’s… fine, just not that bright “can’t-wait” buzz I used to get.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Like, if he spits up a lot or won’t settle, I’ll think maybe I ate the “wrong” thing or I’m not holding him the right way. I know logically it’s not really my fault, but those thoughts still pop in—maybe every other day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes my heart just races out of nowhere—like I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly I’m sure something awful is about to happen to the baby. It passes pretty fast, maybe five or ten minutes, but it’s happened a handful of times this week.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… once or twice I’ve gotten that sudden rush—like my chest tightens and I feel shaky even though nothing’s happening. It’s quick, maybe a minute or two, but it’s unsettling. I just rock the baby and breathe until it fades.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days it feels like the to-do list keeps growing faster than I can tick things off—laundry, bottles, texts I haven’t answered. I usually manage to get through it, but I’ll feel a bit tense or overwhelmed for an hour or two before I can talk myself down and move on.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really. I’m tired enough that once I finally lie down I drift off okay. Maybe once this week I lay there an extra twenty minutes replaying the day, but I wouldn’t say I couldn’t sleep because I was unhappy.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I’d say three or four days this week I’ve had stretches where I just feel kind of heavy and teary. It’s not all day—maybe an hour here or there—but the sadness shows up most afternoons when the house gets quiet.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I’ve cried a couple of times—once when the baby wouldn’t nap and once when I dropped a plate. It wasn’t all-day sobbing, just sudden tears that stopped after a few minutes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that has crossed my mind.

You've shared that, while you can still laugh and complete daily tasks, the joy feels "muted," and several afternoons each week you feel heavy, teary, and overwhelmed by ordinary chores. Sudden <sym>racing heart</sym> worries pop up, yet you soothe yourself and no thoughts of self-harm have appeared.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 12, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient still plans activities but reports a clear reduction in anticipatory pleasure, describing the feeling as "watered-down" and missing the "can't-wait" buzz, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blaming thoughts occurring "every other day," matching "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense anxiety episodes occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sudden intense physical anxiety episodes that recur, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 12 places you in the high-probability range for <med>postpartum depression</med> according to EPDS guidelines. You described <sym>reduced anticipatory pleasure</sym>, multiple days of <sym>low mood</sym> and <sym>tearfulness</sym>, repeated <sym>unwarranted guilt</sym>, and brief <sym>panic-like episodes</sym>, meeting several <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Because sleep is preserved and functioning remains, symptoms appear moderate. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> within the next two weeks to review these results and consider treatment options
2. Continue self-soothing strategies such as paced breathing when <sym>anxiety</sym> spikes; practice twice daily for three cycles of 3-2-3 counts
3. Share your EPDS result with your partner or a trusted family member so they can offer extra support and help monitor mood changes
4. Arrange a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track progress
5. Keep a brief daily log of mood, crying episodes, and any <sym>panic sensations</sym> to discuss with your provider
6. Maintain basic postpartum health: nutritious snacks, hydration, and at least one 20-minute outdoor walk daily
7. Reach out immediately if thoughts of self-harm develop or mood worsens before your appointment
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Summary

Symptoms / concerns endorsed  
- Subjective low mood 3–4 days/week, “heavy and teary”  
- Reduced enjoyment/anticipation (“watered-down” excitement)  
- Intermittent excessive self-blame (every other day)  
- Anxious arousal: sudden racing heart, sense of impending harm, brief panic sensations (episodes lasting seconds–10 min, multiple times/week)  
- Feeling intermittently overwhelmed by daily tasks; tension lasting 1–2 hrs  
- Two discrete crying episodes in past week  
- Sleep generally preserved; no self-harm ideation reported

Observed patterns  
Mood and anxiety symptoms cluster in late afternoon/evening; functional coping remains intact (completing tasks, self-soothing). No current safety concerns.

Screening significance  
Findings suggest mild–moderate depressive symptoms with co-occurring anxiety features; fall within the “possible” range for postpartum depression/anxiety. Recommend completion of a validated rating scale (e.g., EPDS) and follow-up assessment to clarify severity and need for additional support.
